planting.note: Set out divisions or containerized offsets after the last frost into rich, well-drained soil in deep to partial shade, sheltered from wind and direct sun.

directions: Koban is a prized Japanese cultivar of the common lady palm, selected for unusually broad, rounded leaflets that are noticeably wider and fewer per fan than the species type, giving each cane a bold, sculptural silhouette favored by collectors and shade-garden designers. Grow it in humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep to partial shade, since strong sun scorches the wide leaf blades; a mostly shaded courtyard or understory planting suits it best. It is slow to bulk up, sending new canes from an underground rhizome over several years, so patience and division from an established clump are the practical ways to propagate it rather than seed. Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, protect the root zone with mulch, and bring potted specimens indoors before temperatures drop into the mid-20s Fahrenheit, as Koban holds the same cold tolerance limits as straight species Rhapis excelsa.
sources: Pacific Northwest Palm and Exotic Plant Society

common_name: Black Magic Ti Plant (Near-Black Purple Cordyline)

planting.note: Transplant container-grown plants after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade, shielding the dark foliage from harsh midday sun.

directions: Black Magic carries some of the darkest foliage in the ti plant group, unfurling deep maroon-purple leaves that mature to an almost black-bronze sheen under bright, filtered light. Site it in partial shade with morning sun and afternoon protection; too much direct sun can fade the near-black color toward a duller brown, while too little light pushes the leaves toward plain green. Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and keep it consistently moist through the growing season, tapering off watering in cooler months. Use it as a dramatic dark accent against chartreuse or variegated tropical companions such as golden shrimp plant or variegated ginger, and overwinter potted specimens indoors in zones below 9b since it shares the species' intolerance of frost.

common_name: Florida Red Ti Plant (Classic Deep Red-Purple Cordyline)

planting.note: Set out after the last frost into rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun for the deepest, most even leaf coloring.

directions: Florida Red is one of the oldest and most reliable landscape ti plant selections grown throughout the Gulf South, valued for broad, leathery leaves that emerge coppery-bronze and deepen to a rich wine-red to burgundy-purple as they mature. It tolerates more sun than many other ti cultivars, performing well in filtered sun to partial shade, though color intensifies with a bit of afternoon shade in peak summer heat. Grow it in fertile, well-drained soil and water regularly during the growing season, allowing the top inch to dry between waterings in winter. Because it forms sturdy upright canes over time, older clumps can be cut back hard in spring to encourage fresh, more compact colorful growth from the base, and offshoots can be divided to propagate new plants.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Electric Pink Ti Plant (Hot Pink Variegated Cordyline)

planting.note: Plant after the last frost in bright, filtered light and fertile, well-drained soil to bring out the strongest pink variegation.

directions: Electric Pink is grown for its vivid, hot-pink-margined leaves splashed over a green base, giving the foliage a glowing, almost neon two-tone effect that stands out against darker tropical plantings. Bright, filtered light or a few hours of gentle morning sun brings out the most saturated pink coloring, while deep shade mutes the variegation toward plain green and too much hot afternoon sun can scorch the thinner pink leaf tissue. Grow it in humus-rich, well-drained soil, water regularly to keep the root zone evenly moist, and feed lightly through the warm season to sustain vigorous colorful new growth. It stays more compact than many ti plant cultivars, making it a good choice for mixed containers or as a colorful edging plant along a shaded tropical bed, and it should be moved indoors or given heavy protection wherever winter lows approach freezing.

common_name: Ti Amo Ti Plant (Compact Pink and Green Cordyline)

planting.note: Transplant after the last frost into well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade; the compact habit suits containers as well as garden beds.

directions: Ti Amo is a compact, patio-friendly ti plant selection with slender leaves streaked in shades of rose-pink, cream, and green, giving a softer, more pastel variegation than the bolder red or near-black cultivars in the group. Its smaller, denser habit makes it especially well suited to container culture on shaded porches and patios as well as mixed tropical borders where space is limited. Grow it in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to bright indirect light, watering enough to keep the soil consistently moist without letting it become soggy. Because the variegated leaf tissue is more prone to sunburn than solid-colored cultivars, keep it out of direct hot afternoon sun and bring container specimens indoors well before the first frost, as it shares the cold sensitivity typical of Cordyline fruticosa.
